Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 359 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2022) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 359 is located in west-central Alberta, covering an area of 3311 km2. The unit is bounded by 
the Peace River Valley to the north, the border with British Columbia to the west, Highway 49 to the south, and Highway 2 to 
the east. The habitat is dominated by agricultural cropland interspersed with dry mixed wood vegetation.  
An aerial survey for moose and deer was last conducted in 2015 using stratified distance sampling methods. The goal of this 
year’s (2022) survey was to assess the status of moose and deer since the last survey in 2015. Specific objectives were to 
determine a population estimate, population ratio for sex and age classes, a density estimate for moose and mule deer, and a 
directed total count for elk in WMU 359. 
Survey method 
The aerial survey for moose, deer and elk in WMU 359 was conducted from January 18 to 21, 2022. Distance sampling 
methods (Buckland et al., 2001) were used to determine moose and deer population and density estimates. Distance sampling 
transects (n = 314), up to 10 km in length and oriented north-south, were established throughout the unit with 1.2 km spacing. 
A random sample (n = 126) of available transects was flown. The unit was stratified into 2 strata: River Valley (including a 
2000m buffer from the top of break); and Non-River Valley strata. Additional transects were assigned in the River Valley 
stratum to improve the precision of estimates for both species of deer. Moose and deer were classified by age (adult or young) 
and sex. Antler classes were assigned to both species of deer and moose (small, medium, large), and elk (maximum point 
estimates).  
Standard random sampling methods do not reliably estimate elk densities because elk populations are highly clumped. 
Therefore, while all elk observed during the distance sampling transects are classified and counted, an additional dedicated 
survey to locate elk groups not observed on transects was flown to improve the dedicated total counts. This additional effort 
focused on areas where elk are known to occur, have been observed (e.g. tracks or crop damage) or areas with high quality 
habitat that were not surveyed during the transects. 
Results 
All available transects were flown for a total survey effort of 847.25 km and 38.6 hours of flight time (including both the 
distance sampling transects and the dedicated elk inventory).  
In total, 593 moose were observed from 389 independent groups. Of the 592 moose that were successfully classified, 302 
were cows, 163 were calves and 111 were bulls. Of the bulls observed, 18.0% had already shed their antlers. Of the bulls still 
with antlers (n=20), 19 were small (small spike or forked antlers), and 1 was medium (small palmated antler ‘paddles’). The 
bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.37 (90% CI 0.30 – 0.43) and 0.54 (90% CI 0.49 – 0.60), respectively. The density estimate 
was 1.29 moose/km2 with a coefficient of variation of 11.4% (90% CI 1.07 – 1.56). The estimated moose population for WMU 
359 is 4277 (90% CI 3542 - 5165). See Table 1 for a comparison to previous survey results.  
In total, 569 mule deer were observed from 186 independent groups. Of the 418 mule deer that were successfully classified, 
there were 185 does, 137 fawns and 96 bucks. Of the bucks observed, 4% were antlerless, 43% were small (1 or 2 points), 
35% were medium (3 or four points on at least one antler) and 18% were large (at least 4 points, with an antler spread beyond 
the ears). The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.52 (90% CI 0.39 – 0.65) and 0.74 (90% CI 0.66 – 0.82), respectively. The 
density estimate was 0.76 mule deer/km2 with a coefficient of variation of 15.8% (90% CI 0.59 – 0.99). The estimated mule 
deer population for WMU 359 is 2530 (90% CI 1951 - 3280). See Table 2 for a comparison to previous survey results.

We observed 54 white-tailed deer from 26 groups. Of the 47 that were successfully classified, there were 28 antlerless deer, 
and 19 fawns. No antlered deer were observed in the sample. The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.00 and 0.68 
respectively. A reliable density estimate was not possible (90% CI between 278-1113 white-tailed deer, N=550, CV 35.5%). 
See Table 3 for a comparison to previous survey results. 
A total of 1863 elk in 101 groups were observed from transects and focused search flights (approximately 8 hours of additional 
flying time). Of the 972 elk that were successfully classified, 442 were cows, 366 were calves, 239 were unclassified adults, 
and 164 were bulls. Of the bulls observed, 80% were small (1 or 2 point), 13% were medium (3 to 5 point) and 7% were large 
(six point or greater). At this time of year, most bull elk still have antlers so these proportions should be representative of the 
population post-hunting season. The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.37 and 0.59, respectively.
